data.name: Thad
data.long_meaning:
In Hebrew, Thadh is derived from the Hebrew name Thadheus, which means 'courageous'. It is believed to have been borne by several figures in Christian history, including Thaddeus of Edessa, a disciple of Christ, and Thaddeus of Arabia, a companion of St. George.
In the Bible, Thaddeus is one of the twelve apostles, and is mentioned in the New Testament as 'Thaddaeus, the son of Judas, or Lebbaeus, of the tribe of Judah' (Matthew 10:3).
The name Thad is a modern variation of Thaddeus, and carries the same meaning and significance in Christian tradition.

historical_references.reference: Thaddeus of Edessa was a prominent bishop and theologian in the late 4th and early 5th centuries. He is best known for his role in the Christological controversies of the time, particularly his opposition to Nestorianism. Thaddeus was a disciple of Nestorius, but later rejected his master's teachings and became a leading advocate of the Chalcedonian creed. He was born in Edessa, in present-day Turkey, and his writings were influential in shaping the Christological theology of the Eastern Orthodox Church.

historical_references.reference: Thaddeus of Mopsuestia was a prominent theologian and bishop in the late 4th century. He was a leading proponent of the Anti-Chalcedonian position, which rejected the doctrine of the two natures of Christ. Thaddeus was born in Mopsuestia, in present-day Turkey, and his writings were influential in shaping the theology of the Oriental Orthodox Churches. He is best known for his views on the human and divine natures of Christ, which were considered heretical by the Chalcedonian Church.
